description: ORG-E is a five-member interdisciplinary team with backgrounds in Physics, Computer Science, Design, and Engineering. Our strengths are physics, programming, and software development. We combine analytical thinking, creativity, and rapid prototyping to develop practical solutions. Focused on space exploration and Earth sciences, we aim to deliver innovative results for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenges and compete for the top position.
summary: Sky Quest is a free web tool that turns real NASA SPHEREx infrared images into a flip book, so anyone can catch what moves or changes in the sky. SPHEREx re-images the whole sky every six months, but comparing those images over time normally takes FITS files, archive queries and expert software. Sky Quest removes those barriers. Our service fetches SPHEREx cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA and its open copy on AWS, aligns them and stacks them by visit. In the browser, the visits play on their own; users click a dot to measure its shift and brightness, and the result is checked against Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 and explained in plain words. Five practice cases built on the challenge's test targets (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) each teach one tool, with hints, case tokens and a badge earned only when the measurement matches the catalog. Realistic mode then opens all six detectors, real units, a 102-channel spectrum and free exploration of any coordinates. By making SPHEREx time-domain data approachable, Sky Quest invites students, teachers and citizen scientists to join the search for fast-moving stars, cold brown dwarfs and hidden worlds.
details:
What it does.

Sky Quest is a "blink comparator" for the SPHEREx era. It shows the same patch of sky as SPHEREx saw it on different visits and flips between them, so a moving or changing source stands out. It works the way Pluto was found in 1930, but with modern infrared all-sky data. Users can:

- Watch the visits play automatically, or switch to the Difference view (each visit minus the first) and the Stack view.

- Click a source to measure its shift, its speed in each visit, and its brightness through aperture photometry, with uncertainties.

- Read the result in plain language, checked against the Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 positions moved to the visit date. Example for Barnard's Star: "11″ ± 3.7″ in 12 months; catalog 10.2″, consistent within the uncertainty."

Two modes.

- Game mode: a 4-step first-visit tour and 5 practice cases built on the challenge's test targets, each teaching one tool (blink, band choice, magnifier and pixel grid, difference image, light curve). It adds hints, an "I can't find it, show me" button, case tokens, a Sharp Eye badge and a field report. Answers are computed from the data, never typed by hand: expected position = catalog position + proper motion × time; brightness change = photometry compared with noise.

- Realistic mode: all six SPHEREx detectors, values in MJy/sr and mJy, quality and flag layers, saturation and blending warnings, a 102-channel spectrum, CatWISE and Gaia overlays with proper-motion significance, free exploration of any coordinates or object names (SIMBAD), and a candidate notebook with CSV export.

Benefits and impact.

Comparing images is repetitive work, and newcomers drop out fast when they don't know what to do. A study of seven Zooniverse projects and 100,386 volunteers (Sauermann & Franzoni, PNAS 2015) found that most volunteers give a project little time. Sky Quest lowers that barrier: no account, no install, English and Turkish, light and dark themes, and every view is a shareable link that can also be embedded on a school website. The tool is for curious people, teachers and classes, and volunteer hunters of brown dwarfs and high-proper-motion stars.

How it works and the tools we used.

- Data pipeline (Python 3.12): downloads SPHEREx Level 2 cutouts (DR1, QR3 and deep collections) from NASA/IPAC IRSA and keeps a verified local cache. It was checked to be byte-identical on two independent machines. A faster path reads only the needed bytes from the public AWS copy (nasa-irsa-spherex) with HTTP range requests: about 1.8 MB per image instead of 65 MB. Its pixels and flags were identical to IRSA's cutouts. A new sky patch with three detectors now takes about 2–3 minutes instead of about 15.

- Imaging module (NumPy, Astropy): removes zodiacal light, masks bad pixels, uses its own TAN WCS, resamples bilinearly onto a grid twice as fine as the detector, and stacks each visit with sigma clipping. It recovered Barnard's Star's proper motion within 1 %.

- Backend (FastAPI): serves numeric patches (/api/patch), spectra, light curves, Gaia/CatWISE lookups and name resolution. Responses are gzipped and cached on disk. Spectra are measured from cutouts kept in memory, in 0.2–1.3 s instead of 16 s. A refresh command picks up new SPHEREx images as they are published.

- Frontend (React 19, TypeScript, Vite): canvas rendering, measurement and the answer key, with saved copies of the five cases so the demo also works when the archive is unavailable.

- Tests: 88 backend, 27 imaging and 137 frontend automated tests.

Creativity.

The game's answer key runs on the same code as the scientific measurements, so practice cases teach real methods on real data. The badge cannot be earned by guessing.

Factors we considered.

Scientific honesty: saturation, blending and flagged pixels are shown, not hidden. Accessibility for beginners. Speed. Reproducible data. Use of public data only. Graceful fallback when the archive is unavailable. Next steps: fetch new data releases automatically, run guided hunts in fields with no known answer, and pass strong candidates to scientists.
